summary:
Wyoming's facilities law is the most immediate exposure for a trans visitor. House Bill 72, the "Protecting privacy in public spaces act," was signed by Governor Mark Gordon on 3 March 2025 after passing the House 52-8 on 7 February 2025 and the Senate 25-6, and took effect 1 July 2025. It defines male and female by biological sex and requires public facilities to reserve multi-occupancy restrooms, changing areas and sleeping quarters exclusively for males or exclusively for females, prohibiting entry into a facility that does not match biological sex. Accommodations are permitted only where they do not include access to opposite-sex multi-occupancy facilities. The law creates a cause of action against a facility that permitted, or failed to prohibit, an opposite-sex person in a sex-designated restroom or changing area, and a separate cause of action for a person required by a correctional or educational facility to share sleeping quarters with the opposite sex.

A companion measure, Senate File 62, "Sex-designated facilities and public schools," requires public school students from pre-kindergarten upward, including charter school students, to use restrooms aligned with sex assigned at birth, and requires districts to provide a "reasonable accommodation" to any student who does not wish to use a multiple-occupancy restroom or locker room matching the gender at that student's birth. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records the Wyoming facility bans as signed in March 2025.

Wyoming has no state law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations or credit and lending. As of 12 October 2026 the Movement Advancement Project rates the state's gender-identity policy score at -9 out of 25 and its overall score at -6.5 out of 47, a Negative rating. The only recourse for gender-identity employment discrimination is federal. Jackson, Casper and Laramie have ordinances prohibiting discrimination covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations; Cheyenne and Gillette prohibit city employment discrimination on sexual orientation only.

Wyoming has no state hate-crime statute. Debate after the 1998 murder of Matthew Shepard near Laramie did not produce one.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned under a measure passed by both houses in March 2024 and signed by the governor, effective 1 July 2024, barring sexual reassignment surgery and gender-affirming care for children. A separate measure passed in March 2023, which became law without the governor's signature or veto and took effect 1 July 2023, bans transgender students from playing on female sports and athletics teams.

Partner recognition is settled. Same-sex marriage has been recognised in Wyoming since 21 October 2014, after state officials declined to appeal the 17 October federal decision in Guzzo v. Mead striking down the statutory ban; a trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry and have that marriage recognised on the same terms as any other. Private consensual sexual conduct is not criminalised: Wyoming decriminalised consensual sodomy in February 1977 and abrogated common-law liability for anal intercourse in 1982, and the age of consent is 17 for all consensual sexual activity.

Legislative targeting of trans adults continues. An independent legal-risk assessment published in July 2026, drawing on five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric for the worst bills, lists Wyoming among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults.
tangentialFactors:
Repeated attempts to add sexual-orientation protections to Wyoming law failed: a bill was rejected by the House on 31 January 2011, by the Senate 15-13 on 31 January 2013, and a further bill approved 24-6 by the Senate and 6-2 in House committee in February 2015 was rejected 26-33 by the House on 24 February 2015. A 2013 domestic partnership bill providing immediate-family rights was approved 7-2 in House committee on 28 January and rejected 24-35 by the full House on 30 January.

A state obscenity-material law affecting certain LGBT books was enforced in October 2021, when a Gillette librarian was charged by the district attorney and sheriff's office.
localsOnly:
Changing the gender marker on a Wyoming birth certificate requires undergoing sex reassignment surgery and obtaining a court order stating that sex has been changed. The application to Vital Statistics Services must include a letter requesting the change, a photocopy of current identification, a certified copy of the court order, and a doctor's letter confirming the surgery was performed.

Correcting the gender marker on a driver's licence or state identification requires a completed Gender Designation Change Request Form signed by the applicant and by a physician, therapist, counsellor, psychiatric social worker or other medical or social service provider confirming gender identity.

Married couples, including those read as same-sex under birth-sex status, may adopt, and lesbian couples can access in vitro fertilisation; state law recognises the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent after donor insemination irrespective of marital status.

State law neither authorises nor prohibits gestational surrogacy contracts, leaving review case by case. An August 2021 law legalising surrogacy contracts uses the terms mother and father rather than parent or parents, excluding single people and couples read as same-sex.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources differ on the signing date of House Bill 72, giving 3 March 2025 and April 2025; the effective date of 1 July 2025 is consistent across them. Whether the private right of action the law creates has been exercised, and how facilities are applying the ban in practice, is not sourced.

Whether the 2024 restriction on gender-affirming care for minors is currently in force or subject to an injunction is not established in the available sources. The policy scores cited are dated 12 October 2026 and do not capture later changes.
